poems.text:
The year turns down its page, a fading gold,
And swallows chart their long and silent way;
The fields, once warm, are now a story told
In stubble gray beneath a lingering day.
The garden’s last, late rose surrenders breath
To winds that carry rumors of the frost;
Each bough lets go its hold, and what was health
Becomes a memory, lovely and soon lost.
Yet I, who watch the quiet world unbind,
Find no despair in what must fall and flee;
The heart, like earth, must leave its bloom behind
To learn the patience of the coming tree.
So let this parting be a gentle art—
I keep the warmth, and let the season start.

The orchard’s last, bruised apple drops its hold,
And creaking branches bare their knuckled bone;
The wind, a keeper now grown gray and cold,
Unlocks the gate where summer’s warm light shone.

Set sail upon the gutter’s shallow tide,

When dew hung heavy on the hillside’s pride.

The slow, deliberate closing of a door,
The settling of dust in a sunlit space,
The harvest’s weight laid down upon the floor.
So let the season’s rigor have its way;
I’ll keep the ember’s glow for darker day.

poems.text:
The streetlight hums a pale and constant note,
The asphalt gleams with rain that fell at noon.
A single window, high above, afloat,
Holds back the dark with one unsteady moon.
The traffic’s distant pulse, a muted drum,
Beats time for no one walking here but me.
The empty benches wait for hours to come,
And storefront glass repeats what I can’t see.
This solitude is not a thing to fear,
But like a room where echoes learn their name;
The city breathes, and I am merely here,
A leaf that drifted from a hidden flame.
So let the night unspool its silent thread—
I’ll walk until the stars have gone to bed.

The streetlamp hums its thin and jaundiced song,
A weary chorus to the sleeping stone.
The city's breath is shallow, held too long,
And I am utterly, and quite alone.
My footsteps make a lonely, ticking sound
That bounces off the glass and fades to null,
As if the dark were swallowing the ground
On which I walk, a pathway rendered null.
A single window glows a sulfur square,
A distant ship upon a sea of black.
I do not know the soul who kindles there,
Nor does he know the ghost that wanders back.
So I will keep this vigil, cold and deep,
And hold my solitude till morning's keep.

poems.text:
The well of years is deep, and I descend
By crumbling steps where moss and silence meet,
To find the waters that my youth would spend,
A quiet current, cold against the feet.
Each ripple is a face I used to know,
A voice that bends the light of what has been,
And in the glass, the shadows come and go—
The rain that fell, the river's unseen skin.
I cup my hands to hold what will not stay,
The liquid moment slipping through my grip,
And what I drink is only yesterday,
A taste of salt upon the waiting lip.
So let the stream go on, and let it be—
The memory of water stays in me.

poems.text:
The river keeps what daylight cannot hold,
A sunken bell of hours, a coin of years,
And in its murk, a story half-told,
That drifts on currents, deaf to falling tears.
I wade where the shallows ripple, and sift
The silt for a face that the flood erased,
My fingers net a glint, a patient gift—
A shard of mirror where a smile was placed.
But the water tightens, a cold, closing fist,
And the glass slips back to the breathing mud,
Where the shape that I chased no longer exists,
Only the ache of a remembered flood.
So I walk the bank, and the current goes,
While the river keeps what my heart bestows.

And every wave a thrice-remembered plea
From coasts the sunken years have ceased to keep.

Through fathoms where the drowned days turn and gleam,

Unravels what the patient deep has spun—
The bright particular grief I used to bear
Comes surfacing, a ghost beneath the sun,
And I must drink that brine, must taste the whole
Cold archive of the water in my soul.

Where every sunken face I knew is kept;
I drag the river’s hem, the silted mass
Of hours that the living currents swept.
